<!-- SOURCE_TURN_003_BEGIN -->
In the UK, the Harvest festival is celebrated in the autumn, and it marks the end of the farming season. The traditional Harvest festival dance is one of the customs that are still observed in some parts of the country. 

The Harvest dance was traditionally performed in the form of a procession around the fields, and it is believed to have originated from pagan rituals. During the dance, villagers would dress up in costumes and carry wreaths made of wheat and other crops. They would then perform a series of steps and movements that symbolize the processing of the crops.

The dance was accompanied by music played on instruments such as the fiddle, accordion, or pipes. In some areas, it was also common for people to sing songs during the dance.

Today, some villages still observe the Harvest festival with traditional dances. These are often performed by local dance groups and are a way to celebrate the end of the farming season and the bounty of the harvest.
<!-- SOURCE_TURN_003_END -->

Yes, there are many regional variations of the Harvest festival dance in the UK. Often, the specific dances and customs associated with the Harvest festival vary from village to village and region to region, depending on local traditions and influences.

For example, in the county of Somerset in southwest England, there is a tradition of performing the "Hobby Horse Dance" during the Harvest festival. This dance involves a person dressed in a horse costume with a head made of paper-mache, who dances around the village accompanied by music from a harmonica or accordion. The dance is said to have originated as a way of scaring off evil spirits and bringing good luck for the harvest.

In some northern counties, such as Yorkshire, it is traditional to perform the "Pace Egg Play" during the Harvest festival. This involves a group of performers enacting a play that culminates in a battle between the "hero" and "villain" characters, accompanied by music and dance. 

In other regions, such as East Anglia, there is a tradition of performing "Plough Monday" during the Harvest festival. This involves a group of performers dressed in ploughman's costumes, who dance around the village carrying a plough and a straw bear. The dance is said to represent the ploughing and sowing of the fields in preparation for the harvest.

These are just a few examples of the regional variations of the Harvest festival dance in the UK. Each region has its own unique customs and traditions, making the Harvest festival a diverse and rich celebration of the end of the harvest season.
<!-- SOURCE_TURN_011_END -->
